A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MovieRecapsQA and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched reliably, including the renumbered appendix prompts.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of seven multimodal models, a five-participant human study on 118 questions, and modality ablations in Tables 4–5 and S7–S9.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds human semantic-metric scores and a model-response case study.

M1.justification: The alignment, fact extraction, QA generation, question simplification, and claim-based evaluation procedures remain unchanged. Naming GPT-4.1 mini as the judge adds implementation information without establishing a change of judge or scoring procedure.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same 8,231-question, 60-film benchmark with the same modality and reasoning categories. The alternative full-recap and full-movie settings emphasized in v2 already appear in v1 Appendix D; no additional evaluation under those settings is reported.

E2.justification: The seven QA models, human comparators, and semantic and reference-based evaluation methods are retained. Table 4 fills previously missing metric entries for the existing human comparator rather than introducing a distinct competing method.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 newly reports checking GPT-4.1 mini against GPT-4.1 as an alternative evaluator configuration, without specifying the comparison sample or procedure. The existing zero-shot inputs, modality conditions, 118-question human sample, and five participants remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Table S11 illustrates all seven models' responses to one question, their extracted claims, and claim-level judgments. Section 4.2 also adds a qualitative judge-consistency check. The existing modality ablations, alignment examples, and coherence analysis are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both use the same mean-plus-variance reporting in Tables 4 and S7. The new human scores follow this existing practice; v2 adds no seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Its new discussion of variance changes interpretation, not statistical reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Table 4 adds average/best human ROUGE-L scores of 0.16/0.19 and BERTScore scores of 0.88/0.87. Table S11 adds response-level outcomes, and Section 4.2 reports comparable scores from the two judges. Existing tabulated model scores remain unchanged. Section 6.3 newly quotes open-source frames-only factuality as 3.15, although Table 5 implies 3.05 + 0.08 = 3.13.

T1.justification: The atomic-fact and claim-set definitions, scoring rubrics, and Appendix D input formulations are unchanged. Neither version adds theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The benchmark and reference-free metric remain the principal contributions. However, v2's abstract and introduction replace the emphasis on character and narrative-reasoning failures with the claim that visual perception, rather than reasoning, is the primary bottleneck, and assert that only the proposed metric provides meaningful human-aligned separation.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds interpretations that higher score variance demonstrates sensitivity to answer quality and that proprietary models' advantage comes from stronger language priors. It also strengthens the attribution of errors to visual perception and disruptive visual inputs. These extend interpretations of retained results without new controlled tests isolating those explanations.

D1.justification: v2 identifies GPT-4.1 mini as the reference-free judge and explains its cost motivation. The introduction's release link changes from a GitHub repository to the project website. Existing construction details, prompts, and data-release restrictions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work positioning are retained. Although the abstract recasts the novelty statement as the first reference-free open-ended VideoQA benchmark, v1 Section 2 already makes the corresponding distinction. Bibliographic edits do not introduce new research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, metric motivation, and results discussion are rewritten. Section 4 gains a Baseline Metrics subsection, and Section 6 is reorganized around eight numbered observations. This is extensive narrative revision despite largely stable experiments and appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds the color-coded claim-evaluation Table S11, moving the unchanged final prompts to Tables S12–S14. Figures 1–2 are resized, Table 1 moves to page 4, and other tables are repositioned. Existing figure content and most table structures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity and reproducibility by identifying the judge, clarifying the evaluated setting, and adding human scores and a worked example. However, stronger claims about human-preference alignment and perception rather than reasoning lack corresponding validation. New Table S11 also gives Gemini relevance 2 despite labeling every claim irrelevant, conflicting with Table S13's score-0 rule. These documentation gains and scientific consistency problems leave the net quality effect unclear.
